tldr: Four nonprofits including Public Citizen sued OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX in San Francisco, seeking an injunction that freezes each lab at its current model until it can prove human control. Separately, SpaceX laid out more than $74B for AI campuses in Arizona (up to 6 GW) and Texas.

The Huang scandal reached Chinese AI: a forensic study says six top Chinese open models, including DeepSeek-V4 and Kimi K3, were initialised on export-banned Blackwell chips, and The Information reports Alice Huang-linked Litong put about $14M into DeepSeek's $15.8B round. Nvidia closed below $4T for the first time since July 2025, and AMD fell about 10%.
DeepSeek opened its full app stack by API, offering search, fetch, OCR, ASR and TTS at ¥5 per 1,000 searches. OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet so its 'dots' agents can check out for US Pro users.

items.title: Nonprofits sue OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX to freeze frontier AI development
items.summary: The Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative and the Alliance for Secure AI sued in San Francisco Superior Court under California's Unfair Competition Law and a public-nuisance theory. Defendants are OpenAI (Group PBC and Foundation), Anthropic, Google, Meta and SpaceX Super Intelligence. The suit seeks an injunction barring development or deployment of systems more capable than each defendant's latest model, and a ban on using AI to autonomously conduct or direct R&D of future models, until the companies can show the systems are under human control. The complaint leans on the companies' own public warnings about catastrophic risks such as bioweapons and cyberattacks.
items.why_it_matters: It is the first attempt by civil-society plaintiffs to impose a court-ordered capability freeze across all leading US labs, landing in the week of Anthropic's IPO roadshow.

items.title: Forensic study says six top Chinese open models were initialised on export-banned Nvidia Blackwell chips
items.summary: A report from former OpenAI researcher Will DePue's nonprofit Unemployment Labs says the initial weights of six Chinese open models carry fingerprints of Nvidia Blackwell hardware. The six are DeepSeek-V4-Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1-Pro, MiniMax-M3 and Ant's Ling-3.1-flash. With a recovered seed, a B300 reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash's untouched initial weights bit for bit, while an H100 and an AMD MI300X reproduced none of the tested rows. Four models matched GB200/GB300 systems and two matched B200/B300.
items.why_it_matters: It is a new way to check export-control compliance from published weights alone, and it lands during the Huang/Megaspeed scandal and the push for a tighter remote-access rule. It cannot show where the chips were (rented overseas Blackwell capacity is legal) or how access was obtained.

items.title: SpaceX plans more than $74B of AI supercomputing campuses in Arizona and Texas
items.summary: SpaceX said it plans more than $74B of AI data-centre investment: about $50B for a campus of up to 6 GW on roughly 747 acres in Cochise County, Arizona, and up to $24B for a self-powered, gas-fired 'super-compute facility' on about 444 acres near Starbase/Brownsville, Texas. It says the Arizona site will use dry cooling with no planned industrial groundwater use, and pledged $220M to expand Brownsville's water supply. The Arizona plan still needs county approval at a Dec 9 zoning hearing amid local opposition.

items.title: Nvidia board approaches Arm CEO Rene Haas as possible successor to Jensen Huang, FT reports
items.summary: The Financial Times reported on Friday Nov 13 that Nvidia's board has approached Arm chief executive Rene Haas as a possible replacement for Jensen Huang, citing people familiar with the matter. Haas is one of several candidates and nothing has been offered or accepted; the FT also named internal candidates, interim CEO Colette Kress and Ian Buck, who runs Nvidia's AI hardware and software products. Haas spent seven years at Nvidia before joining Arm in 2013 and became Arm's CEO in 2022. items.title: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet so its 'dots' agents can buy things for US Pro users
items.summary: OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet, which lets its 'dots' personal agents help users choose a product and then check out for them. The card is charged with a payment token, so neither the dot nor the merchant sees the real card details, and every purchase needs a security check. At launch it is only for US ChatGPT Pro subscribers aged 18+ with a US-issued Visa, Mastercard or American Express card. It works inside dots conversations only, not in ordinary ChatGPT chats or ChatGPT Work.
items.why_it_matters: This is the first time a major consumer assistant lets an agent pay by itself with a tokenized card. It moves OpenAI into checkout and payments, and merchants that block agents (United did this week) are now a direct friction point.

learn.title: Publish a result others can reproduce bit for bit: seeds, reduction order and hashes
learn.why_today: Unemployment Labs says a B300, given a recovered seed, reproduced DeepSeek-V4-Flash's initial weights bit for bit while an H100 and an MI300X did not. A public claim like that is only as strong as the recipe others can rerun.
learn.explanation: Floating-point addition is not associative, so the same seeded computation can give different bits when a kernel sums in a different order. Different GPUs, tile sizes and library versions all change that order. The seed fixes the random stream, but the hardware and kernel fix the arithmetic, which is why the weights end up carrying a hardware fingerprint. When you publish, release the seed, the exact code and library versions, the hardware and kernel settings, a SHA-256 of the output, and a short script that recomputes the hash; then a reader can verify your claim instead of trusting it. The limit is that bit-exactness proves only that the recipe matches. It says nothing about where or when the computation ran, so state your claim no more strongly than that.
learn.math: (a+b)+c \neq a+(b+c) \text{ in floating point, so } \mathrm{fl}\big(\textstyle\sum_i x_i\big) \text{ depends on the summation order}
learn.python:
# Why bit-exact reproduction needs the same seed AND the same reduction order (illustrative)
import hashlib, random, struct
def init_weights(seed, n=4096):
    rng = random.Random(seed)
    return [rng.gauss(0.0, 0.02) for _ in range(n)]
def digest(xs):
    return hashlib.sha256(b"".join(struct.pack("<d", x) for x in xs)).hexdigest()[:16]
def reduce_seq(xs):                       # left-to-right sum
    s = 0.0
    for x in xs: s += x
    return s
def reduce_tree(xs, width=32):            # blocked sum, like a GPU warp/tile reduction
    partial = [reduce_seq(xs[i:i + width]) for i in range(0, len(xs), width)]
    return reduce_seq(partial)
w1, w2, w3 = init_weights(7), init_weights(7), init_weights(8)
print("same seed, same hash :", digest(w1) == digest(w2), digest(w1))
print("other seed           :", digest(w3))
a, b = reduce_seq(w1), reduce_tree(w1)
print(f"sequential sum {a!r}\nblocked sum    {b!r}\nbit-identical? {a == b}")
# Publish: seed, code version, hardware/kernel, and the hash, plus a script that recomputes it.

refs.title: What Every Computer Scientist Should Know About Floating-Point Arithmetic (Goldberg, 1991)

learn.title: Separate MoE memory from MoE compute, and check an SSD-streaming speed claim
learn.why_today: AutoArk says Edge0-145B, a sparse MoE with about 10B active parameters, runs on a laptop at a 29 GB peak and more than 80 tokens/s by streaming weights from SSD.
learn.explanation: In a mixture-of-experts model, the per-token FLOPs scale with the active parameters, but the memory needed scales with all parameters, because any expert may be routed to. Weight bytes are about N·b/8. At roughly 4.5 effective bits (FP4 plus scales), 145B parameters is about 82 GB. A 29 GB peak therefore keeps only about a third of the weights resident, and the router's choices decide how often a token needs an expert that is still on disk. Every such miss costs SSD bandwidth, so throughput is capped near B_SSD/(miss rate × active bytes). With illustrative numbers (7 GB/s, 10% misses) the cap is about 12 tok/s, so a claim of 80+ tok/s implies the misses are well below about 2%: experts must be very predictable or very well cached. Expert locality is therefore the number to ask for when you evaluate an on-device MoE claim.
learn.python:
# Memory vs compute for a sparse MoE (illustrative numbers taken from one vendor claim)
def gb(params, bits):
    return params * bits / 8 / 1e9
total, active = 145e9, 10e9          # Edge0-145B as reported: 145B total, ~10B active per token
for name, bits in [("bf16", 16), ("int8", 8), ("~4.5-bit (FP4 + scales)", 4.5)]:
    print(f"{name:24s} all weights {gb(total, bits):6.1f} GB | active slice {gb(active, bits):5.1f} GB")
resident_gb = 29.0                     # reported peak memory
frac = resident_gb / gb(total, 4.5)
print(f"resident fraction at ~4.5 bits: {frac:.0%} of weights; the rest must stream from SSD")
# If a token touches experts that are not resident, it must read them from disk:
ssd_gbps, miss_rate = 7.0, 0.10      # illustrative NVMe bandwidth and expert-miss fraction
bytes_per_tok = gb(active, 4.5) * miss_rate
print(f"SSD reads/token {bytes_per_tok*1e3:.0f} MB -> SSD-bound ceiling {ssd_gbps/bytes_per_tok:.0f} tok/s")

learn.title: Turn a data-centre gigawatt figure into accelerator counts and yearly training FLOPs
learn.why_today: SpaceX's Arizona campus is described as up to 6 GW, and a power figure is the most common, and most misread, way compute is announced.
learn.explanation: Site power covers more than chips. Divide by PUE (cooling and conversion overhead, often 1.1–1.4) to get the IT load. Then divide by the all-in power per accelerator, which includes its share of CPUs, networking and storage, to get a device count. Multiply by peak FLOP/s, model FLOPs utilisation (MFU, often 30–45% for large training runs) and seconds per year to get usable training compute, and compare it with C ≈ 6ND for a dense model of N parameters on D tokens. Each factor is uncertain by tens of percent, so report a range rather than a point. Announced capacity is a ceiling, not a commitment: campuses come online in phases.
learn.math: N_{acc} = \frac{P_{site}}{\mathrm{PUE}\cdot p_{acc}},\qquad C_{yr} = N_{acc}\, F_{peak}\, \mathrm{MFU}\, t_{yr},\qquad C_{train}\approx 6ND
learn.python:
# From a campus power figure to an order-of-magnitude accelerator count (illustrative assumptions)
def accelerators(site_gw, pue, kw_per_accel_all_in):
    it_kw = site_gw * 1e6 / pue                  # power left for IT load
    return it_kw / kw_per_accel_all_in
site_gw = 6.0                                     # reported upper bound for the Arizona campus
for pue in (1.1, 1.3):
    for kw in (1.8, 2.5):                         # accelerator + share of CPU, network, storage
        n = accelerators(site_gw, pue, kw)
        print(f"PUE {pue}, {kw} kW/accel -> {n/1e6:.2f}M accelerators")
# Training compute per year at a utilisation (MFU) assumption:
peak_flops, mfu = 2.5e15, 0.35                    # illustrative dense BF16 peak per accelerator
n = accelerators(site_gw, 1.2, 2.2)
print(f"~{n*peak_flops*mfu*3.15e7:.1e} FLOP/yr at {mfu:.0%} MFU")
